content: Preventing preterm labor is a critical step in reducing the incidence of preterm birth. Prostaglandins play a significant role in the processes of labor and delivery. The production of prostaglandins can be inhibited by blocking the cyclo-oxygenase (COX) enzyme, which may, in turn, suppress uterine contractions. However, a prior Cochrane review on the use of COX inhibitors for treating preterm labor found insufficient evidence to determine their effectiveness. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of COX inhibitors in preventing preterm labor among women at high risk. The researchers conducted a search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trial Register up to June 30, 2012. They included all randomized trials, both published and unpublished, that assessed the use of any COX inhibitor for preventing preterm labor in pregnant women at less than 36 weeks of gestation who were at risk of, but not actively experiencing, preterm labor. Cluster-randomized trials were eligible for inclusion, but quasi-randomized trials and studies with cross-over designs were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the potential studies for inclusion, resolved disagreements through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer, and evaluated the quality of the trials. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers and subsequently checked for accuracy. The review included one randomized trial involving 98 women, which evaluated the use of a specific COX inhibitor, rofecoxib, for preventing preterm birth. However, the study did not report data on one of the primary outcomes, preterm labor. The use of rofecoxib was associated with an increased risk of preterm birth and preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM). Additionally, rofecoxib was linked to a higher risk of oligohydramnios (reduced amniotic fluid) and decreased fetal urine production, although these effects were reversible upon discontinuation of the treatment. There were no significant differences in the number of women who discontinued treatment before 32 weeks of gestation. Similarly, there were no differences in neonatal morbidities, rates of admission to the neonatal intensive care unit, maternal adverse effects, or perinatal mortalities between the groups. The authors concluded that there is very limited evidence regarding the use of COX inhibitors for preventing preterm labor. The available data are insufficient to support any clinical recommendations for the use of COX inhibitors in this context. Future research should include follow-up studies to assess both the short-term and long-term effects of COX inhibitors on infants.
